speaker: Mike Krieger
title: Anthropic's CPO on what comes next | Mike Krieger
question: At frontier AI companies, why does embedding product teams with model researchers create more leverage than polishing UX around a finished model?
guest: It has continued to be true, and I have become even more convinced of it. If we are shipping things that could have been built by anybody just using our models off the shelf, there is great stuff to be built that way, do not get me wrong. But where we can play uniquely should be stuff right at that magic intersection between the two. For example, we took someone from our post-training team focused on teaching Claude specific skills, paired them with product people, and together we revamped how features look in the product and what Claude can do—way better than just taking the model and prompting it a little bit. That is just not enough; we need to be in the fine-tuning process. The functional unit of work is no longer taking a finished model and working with design and product to ship something. It is being in the post-training conversations around how these things should work, then building, and looping those insights back into training.

points.core: Products built solely by prompting off-the-shelf models lack structural defensibility.
points.note: Accept: thin UI or prompt wrappers on top of general models being easily replicable by any external builder. Do not credit: generic competition platitudes not tied to off-the-shelf prompting.

points.core: Shaping model behavior during post-training unlocks capabilities that prompting alone cannot achieve.
points.note: Accept: co-designing features via fine-tuning, RL, or skill-specific post-training delivering qualitatively stronger product behavior than prompt engineering. Do not credit: vague claims that better models make better products.

points.core: Product development becomes a continuous feedback loop into training rather than a handoff.
points.note: Accept: product teams participating directly in post-training design and feeding product insights back into subsequent training runs instead of receiving a finished model over the wall. Do not credit: generic advice that product and research teams should collaborate closely.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because in AI products the model is the product: most of what users experience as quality, such as capability, reliability, speed, tone, and what tasks are even possible, is determined during training, not in the interface layered on top. UX polish around a frozen model can only reduce friction at the margins; it cannot make the model do something it can't.

Embedding product people with researchers lets them shape the model itself. They bring real user needs and failure cases into training data, evaluations, and fine-tuning targets, so the model improves on what matters rather than on abstract benchmarks. They also see emerging capabilities months early, which lets them design products for where the model is going rather than where it was. Features like tool use, long-context coding, or artifacts-style interfaces came from co-developing a model behaviour and a product surface together.

There is also a durability argument. Each model generation tends to erase wrappers and workarounds built for the last one, while product insight encoded in the model compounds. And tight loops between usage data and research produce a feedback flywheel that competitors working only at the interface layer cannot replicate.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
In frontier AI, the model’s behavior is the core user experience. When product teams only receive a finished model, they must treat it as a fixed black box, spending months building brittle UI scaffolding, prompt workarounds, and guardrails to mask its flaws. Because model capabilities advance rapidly, the next training run often renders that defensive UX work obsolete overnight.

Embedding product teams with researchers replaces this one-way handoff with a tight co-design loop. Product builders translate real user friction and workflow failures directly into evaluations, post-training data, and reinforcement learning environments, fixing limitations in the weights rather than papering over them in the interface. Co-designing the model alongside its runtime harness also lets teams train native behaviors like reliable tool use, calibration, and steerability, creating improvements that compound across every product surface. Finally, embedded product teams spot emergent capabilities while models are still training, allowing them to design new interaction paradigms for where intelligence is heading rather than optimizing interfaces for where it has already been.

noweb.answer:
In frontier AI, the model is not a static backend component—it is the product’s core behavior. Treating a model as finished forces teams to build brittle UX scaffolding, prompt hacks, and rigid guardrails to mask underlying limitations. That surface polish hits a low ceiling and often becomes obsolete—or actively counterproductive—the moment a stronger model ships.

Embedding product teams with researchers turns real user friction directly into training signal. Instead of designing interface workarounds for hallucinations, clumsy tool use, or latency bottlenecks, product insights shape post-training datasets, reinforcement learning environments, and evaluations. Fixing failure modes in the weights eliminates entire layers of UI complexity while lifting every downstream workflow at once. Meanwhile, product builders uncover valuable emergent capabilities that static academic benchmarks miss, guiding research toward practical agency and steerability. Co-designing the model and interface creates a compounding flywheel: live product usage produces sharper evaluations and stronger weights, which in turn unlock simpler, far more capable user experiences than wrapping UX polish around frozen capabilities ever could.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Embedding product people with researchers gives more leverage because at frontier labs the model is the product's main moving part, and it keeps changing. A finished model fixes what the product can do. UX polish can only make those fixed capabilities easier to reach, and the next model release may make that work obsolete. When product teams sit with researchers, what users need can shape the model itself. Real failures from users become training data, evaluations and fine-tuning goals. Product requirements can steer what gets trained, such as tool use, long-context reliability or agentic behavior. Designers also learn early what new capabilities are coming, so they can build interfaces for what the next model will do. Claude Code and ChatGPT's tool-calling features came out of that kind of loop. The feedback cycle also gets much shorter, from release cycles down to training runs. And the lab can find product ideas that only make sense once you know a capability is about to work. Polish still matters, but it adds value in small steps. Shaping the model together with the product is what produces new categories of products.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
At frontier AI companies, the biggest product bottlenecks are usually model capabilities rather than interface polish. When product teams treat a model as a finished artifact, they end up building brittle scaffolding, complex prompts, and UI workarounds to mask failure modes that could be solved far more cleanly in post-training, data curation, or reinforcement learning. Worse, much of that UX polish is quickly obsoleted by the next model release.

Embedding product teams directly with researchers creates a tight co-design loop. Product teams supply real user workflows, edge cases, and high-signal evaluations that steer what the model is actually trained to optimize—such as tool use, instruction following, latency, or multi-step reliability. In return, researchers give product teams early visibility into emerging capabilities, letting them design interfaces for what the next model will unlock rather than compensating for what the current one lacks. Because improvements baked into the model lift every user interaction at once, co-evolving the model and product compounds far faster than polishing the wrapper around a static checkpoint.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Embedding product teams with model researchers lets real user needs shape the model while it’s still being built. Product teams see where users get stuck, which failures break trust, and which tasks are worth a slower or more expensive response. Researchers can turn those observations into evaluations and use them to guide training, tool use, and latency trade-offs. Product teams can then test whether those changes actually help users get their work done.

Polishing the UX around a finished model can make its capabilities easier to access. The bigger leverage comes from improving the capabilities themselves. A clearer interface can help users recover from a failed multi-step task. A model that completes the task reliably saves that recovery work every time, and the same improvement can benefit several products.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Embedding product teams with model researchers shortens the feedback loop between what users need and what the model learns to do. A product team might see users repeatedly correcting a model that loses track of constraints during a long task. Working together, the teams can turn those failures into an evaluation, test changes during training, and see whether users need to intervene less often.

Once a model is finished, better UX can make its capabilities easier to use and help people recover from errors. Changing the model can remove the source of a recurring error across every product that uses it. The collaboration also works in the other direction. Product teams that see an emerging capability early can test which user problems it solves while there’s still time to shape the model.
